column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: The branch of biology that studies fungi is called –
column14: Zoology
column15: Mycology
column16: Ecology
column17: Botany
column28: Mycology is the study of fungi. Botany is the study of plants, and picking it because mushrooms grow in soil like plants is the common mistake.
column29: The word comes from the Greek word for mushroom, myco-.

column9: In 1928, Alexander Fleming discovered the first antibiotic, ___, from a mold growing on his lab dish.
column28: The antibiotic is penicillin, made by the mold Penicillium. Writing Penicillium, the name of the mold itself, is the common mix-up.
column29: The medicine's name sounds almost like the mold's name.

column9: Which word correctly describes how fungi get their food?
column14: Producers, because they capture energy from sunlight
column15: Heterotrophs, because they depend on other organisms for food
column16: Autotrophs, because they make their own food
column17: Autotrophs, because they soak up sunlight through their caps
column28: Fungi are heterotrophs: they get food from other living or dead organisms. Calling them autotrophs or producers like plants is the common mistake; fungi have no chlorophyll.
column29: Hetero- means other. Where does a fungus's food come from?

column9: Fungal cell walls are built from a tough material called chitin. Which other organism also uses chitin?
column14: An oak tree, in its wood
column15: A human, in its bones
column16: A fern, in its leaves
column17: A beetle, in its hard outer shell
column28: Chitin is found in fungal cell walls and in the outer skeletons of insects like beetles. Wood and plant leaves are made with cellulose, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Think of something crunchy that crawls.

column9: A baker adds a living fungus to bread dough to make it rise. Which fungus is it?
column14: Yeast
column15: Penicillium
column16: Bread mold
column17: A puffball
column28: Bakers use yeast. Bread mold is a fungus that spoils bread rather than helping make it, which is the common mix-up.
column29: It comes in little packets in the baking aisle.

column9: Under a microscope, bread mold looks like a tangle of tiny, branching threads. What is each thread called?
column14: A flagellum
column15: A root hair
column16: A spore
column17: A hypha
column28: Each thread of a fungus is a hypha (plural hyphae). Root hairs belong to plants, and fungi have no roots, so that is the common mistake.
column29: The plural of this word is hyphae.

column9: A large, tangled mass of hyphae hidden inside soil or a rotting log is called a –
column14: fruiting body
column15: lichen
column16: mycelium
column17: sporangium
column28: A mass of hyphae is a mycelium. The fruiting body is the part that pokes above the surface, which is the common mix-up.
column29: It is the hidden main body of the fungus.

column9: A mushroom popping up on a rotting log has one main job. What is it?
column14: Absorbing sunlight to make food
column15: Storing water for dry weather
column16: Making and releasing spores
column17: Holding the fungus in place like a root
column28: The mushroom is the fruiting body, and its job is reproduction: it makes and releases spores. Thinking it catches sunlight like a leaf is the common mistake.
column29: Most of the fungus is hidden inside the log. Why would part of it come out into the open air?

column9: Which statement about the number of cells in fungi is correct?
column14: Fungi have no cells; they are made of chitin threads.
column15: Most fungi are multicellular, but yeasts are unicellular.
column16: All fungi are unicellular.
column17: All fungi are multicellular, including yeast.
column28: Most fungi, like mushrooms and molds, are made of many cells, but yeasts are single cells. Saying all fungi are one way or the other is the common mistake.
column29: Think of a mushroom, then think of the fungus in a baking packet.

column9: Why can't a fungus make its own food?
column14: It has no chlorophyll, so it cannot do photosynthesis.
column15: Its chitin cell walls block out all of the sunlight that reaches it.
column16: It only grows at night.
column17: It lives underground, where there is no sunlight or water to use.
column28: Fungi lack chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesize. Many fungi grow in the open air and light, so blaming darkness is the common mistake.
column29: What green pigment do plants use to make food?

column9: Fungi reproduce by making seeds, just like flowering plants.
column28: False. Fungi never make seeds. They reproduce with spores, which are usually single tiny cells with no stored food or embryo inside.
column29: Think about what puffballs release when you squeeze them.

column9: Most fungi are saprophytes. What does a saprophyte feed on?
column14: Only sugar from living plant roots
column15: Living animals that it attacks
column16: Dead or decaying organisms
column17: Sunlight and carbon dioxide
column28: A saprophyte feeds on dead or decaying material. A fungus that attacks a living host is a parasite, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Most fungi are found on rotting things.

column9: In a food web, fungi that break down dead organisms and return nutrients to the soil play the role of ___.
column28: Fungi are decomposers. Writing consumer or producer is the common mistake; producers make food, and fungi cannot.
column29: The word means they de-compose, or break apart, dead things.

column9: Which of these organisms is NOT a fungus?
column14: Mushroom
column15: Moss
column16: Yeast
column17: Bread mold
column28: Moss is a small plant that has chlorophyll and makes its own food. Moss grows in damp, shady places like many fungi, which is why it gets mixed up with them.
column29: Which one is green and makes its own food?

column9: Select every organism that is a fungus. Select all that apply.
column14: Bread mold
column15: Puffball
column16: Kelp
column17: Moss
column28: Puffballs, morels and bread mold are fungi. Moss is a plant, kelp is a protist and staph is a bacterium. Picking moss because it grows on logs with fungi is the common mistake.
column29: Cross out the plant, the protist and the bacterium.

column9: A fungus is growing on an orange. Where is the orange actually being digested?
column14: In the soil, by the roots of nearby plants that absorb it
column15: Inside a small stomach at the base of the fungus
column16: Outside the fungus, by enzymes the hyphae release
column17: Inside chloroplasts in the fungus
column28: Fungi release digestive enzymes onto their food and digest it outside their bodies, then absorb it. Fungi have no stomach, so picturing an animal-style stomach is the common mistake.
column29: A fungus has no mouth. What could it pour onto its food?

column9: Which of these do fungi NOT have?
column14: Cell walls
column15: Roots, stems and leaves
column16: Spores
column17: Nuclei in their cells
column28: Fungi have no true roots, stems or leaves. They do have cell walls (made of chitin), nuclei and spores. A mushroom's stalk looks like a stem, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Which choice lists plant parts?

column9: All fungi are harmful to people.
column28: False. Some fungi cause disease, but others give us foods, bread, cheese and medicines like penicillin, and many recycle nutrients in nature.
column29: Think about pizza toppings and medicine.

column9: Which human illness is caused by a fungus?
column14: Athlete's foot
column15: The flu
column16: Strep throat
column17: Malaria
column28: Athlete's foot is a fungal skin infection. Strep throat is caused by bacteria, the flu by a virus and malaria by a protist.
column29: Which one grows on damp skin between the toes?

column9: Ringworm is an itchy, ring-shaped rash on the skin. What causes it?
column14: A virus
column15: A fungus
column16: A parasitic worm
column17: A bacterium
column28: Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a worm. The name misleads people into picking worm, which is the common mistake.
column29: Don't trust the name.

column9: A mushroom is classified in which kingdom?
column14: Fungi
column15: Protista
column16: Animalia
column17: Plantae
column28: Mushrooms belong to Kingdom Fungi. They grow in soil and don't move, so placing them in Plantae is the common mistake.
column29: Mushrooms have no chlorophyll.

column9: "Fungi" is the plural word. What is the word for just one?
column14: Fungis
column15: Fungum
column16: Fungal
column17: Fungus
column28: One is a fungus; two or more are fungi. Fungal is an adjective, as in a fungal infection, which is the common mix-up.
column29: It ends the same way as cactus.

column9: Which grocery store item is itself a fungus?
column14: A portobello mushroom
column15: A potato
column16: Spinach
column17: A seaweed snack
column28: A portobello is a mushroom, which is a fungus. A potato and spinach are plants, and seaweed is a protist (algae). A potato grows underground like a mycelium, which is a common mix-up.
column29: Which one has a cap and gills?

column9: Blue cheese gets its blue-green veins and sharp flavor from –
column14: a mold, which is a fungus
column15: food coloring made from algae
column16: bacteria that turn milk blue
column17: crushed blueberries
column28: The veins in blue cheese are a Penicillium mold that cheesemakers add on purpose. Bacteria help make cheese too, but the blue color comes from the mold.
column29: Moldy food is usually bad, but this is one time it is on purpose.

column9: A fallen birch log in a Wisconsin forest slowly turns soft and crumbly over several years. Which organisms are doing much of this work?
column14: Deer
column15: Fungi
column16: Mosses
column17: Ferns
column28: Fungi are major decomposers of wood: their hyphae grow through the log and digest it. Mosses often grow on logs, but they make their own food and don't break the wood down.
column29: Which organisms feed on dead wood?

column9: The crusty gray-green patches on an old gravestone are lichens. A lichen is made of –
column14: two kinds of mushrooms grown together into one crust
column15: a bacterium living inside a plant root
column16: a moss and a tiny fern growing together on the stone
column17: a fungus living with an alga or cyanobacteria
column28: A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner (an alga or cyanobacteria). It looks like moss, which is the common mix-up.
column29: One partner can make food from sunlight; the other cannot.

column9: When a fungal spore lands on moist food, a small tube grows out of it and becomes the first hypha. What is this tube called?
column14: A sporangium
column15: A germ tube
column16: A fruiting body
column17: A gill
column28: The first hypha growing out of a spore is the germ tube. Fruiting bodies come much later, after a whole mycelium has formed.
column29: Think of the spore germinating, like a seed sprouting.

column9: Bread mold makes its spores inside tiny round cases on the tips of upright hyphae. These spore cases are called ___.
column28: Spore cases are sporangia (one is a sporangium). Gills are where mushrooms make spores, which is the common mix-up.
column29: The word starts with spor-, like spore.

column9: Which statement about fungal spores is true?
column14: Most are microscopic, so millions can float in the air.
column15: They can only be seen once they are planted in damp soil and swell up.
column16: Most are about the size of a pea.
column17: Each has a hard seed coat and stored food, like a plant seed.
column28: Fungal spores are microscopic, which is why a puffball's "smoke" is millions of spores. Picturing spores as big as seeds is the common mistake.
column29: Can you see a single spore drifting in the air?

column9: Which statement about fungi and sunlight is true?
column14: Fungi die as soon as sunlight touches them, which is why they grow in the dark.
column15: Fungi do not need sunlight, because they absorb food from what they grow on.
column16: Fungi store sunlight inside their spores.
column17: Fungi need bright sunlight to photosynthesize.
column28: Fungi get food by absorbing it, so they can grow in dark places like basements and inside logs. Thinking fungi need light like plants is the common mistake.
column29: Mold can grow in a dark cupboard. What does that tell you?

column9: A student finds white, cottony fuzz on old strawberries. What is the fuzz?
column14: Roots of a tiny plant growing into the fruit
column15: A layer of dust
column16: Crystals of sugar that dried on the skin
column17: Hyphae of a mold growing into the fruit
column28: The fuzz is a mold's hyphae spreading through the strawberries and digesting them. Calling them roots is the common mistake, since fungi have no roots.
column29: What living thing grows on old fruit?

column9: Yeast can reproduce by growing a small bump that pinches off to become a new cell. This kind of reproduction is called ___.
column28: Yeast reproduces by budding: a bud grows and pinches off. Fragmentation is when a piece of hyphae breaks off and grows, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Think of a bud on a branch.

column9: A piece of a fungus's hyphae breaks off, gets carried by rainwater and grows into a new fungus. This shows that fungi can –
column14: make seeds
column15: reproduce from pieces of hyphae
column16: reproduce only with spores
column17: photosynthesize in water
column28: Fungi can grow new individuals from broken pieces of hyphae, not just from spores. Saying fungi only reproduce with spores is the common mistake.
column29: Did a spore or a seed start the new fungus here?

column9: The fungus that causes athlete's foot often grows on the skin between toes. Why is this a good place for it?
column14: It is dry, and fungi need dry places.
column15: It has bits of soil and dirt that the fungus can grow roots into.
column16: It is sunny, so the fungus can photosynthesize.
column17: It is warm and moist, and the fungus can feed on the skin.
column28: Fungi grow best in warm, moist places with food, and sweaty feet in shoes provide all three. Thinking fungi need dry or sunny places is the common mistake.
column29: Think about feet inside sweaty socks and shoes.

column9: Many wild mushrooms in Wisconsin look like edible ones but are deadly. What is the safest rule?
column14: Eat it if it is white.
column15: Never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has identified it.
column16: Eat it if it smells good.
column17: Eat it if animals have nibbled on it, since that shows it is not poisonous.
column28: Some poisonous mushrooms smell fine, are white or are eaten by animals. Only an expert's identification is safe; trusting looks or smell is the common, dangerous mistake.
column29: Some deadly mushrooms look completely harmless.

column9: After a fungus's enzymes break down its food, what does the fungus do with the nutrients?
column14: Turns them into chlorophyll
column15: Packs them all into spores and releases them
column16: Swallows them through a mouth
column17: Absorbs them through the walls of its hyphae
column28: Fungi absorb the digested nutrients through their hyphae. They have no mouth, so picturing swallowing is the common mistake.
column29: The threads are in direct contact with the food.

column9: Select every feature that ALL fungi share. Select all that apply.
column14: Bodies made of many cells
column15: Chlorophyll for photosynthesis
column16: Getting food from other organisms
column17: Eukaryotic cells (with a nucleus)
column28: All fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs with chitin walls. Not all are multicellular (yeast is one cell), and fungi have no chlorophyll or cellulose. Choosing "many cells" is the common mistake.
column29: Think of yeast when you decide about the number of cells.

column9: Mold is growing on a forgotten sandwich in a locker. Where is the mold getting its energy?
column14: From the metal locker
column15: From sunlight
column16: From the sandwich
column17: From the air
column28: The mold is a heterotroph, so it gets energy by digesting and absorbing the sandwich. Thinking it uses light or air like a plant is the common mistake.
column29: What is the mold growing on?

column9: The underside of a mushroom's cap is lined with thin, papery gills. What happens on the gills?
column14: Food is made by photosynthesis.
column15: Roots attach to the soil.
column16: Water is stored for dry weather.
column17: Spores are made and released.
column28: Mushroom gills produce spores that drop out of the cap. Thinking the gills breathe like a fish's or make food like leaves is the common mistake.
column29: The cap is part of the fruiting body. What is that part for?

column9: When people say "a fungus," what is the living main body of a mushroom-forming fungus?
column14: The millions of spores floating in the air
column15: The mycelium, hidden in the soil or wood
column16: The cap of the mushroom, above the ground
column17: The stalk of the mushroom
column28: The main body is the mycelium. The cap and stalk are just the fruiting body, so picking the mushroom itself is the common mistake.
column29: Most of the fungus is out of sight.

column9: Some fungi harm trees. Which tree disease is caused by a fungus?
column14: Chickenpox
column15: Dutch elm disease
column16: Lyme disease
column17: Strep throat
column28: Dutch elm disease is caused by a fungus that has killed millions of elm trees. Lyme disease and strep throat are bacterial, and chickenpox is viral.
column29: Look for the one that infects a tree.

column9: What is penicillin used for?
column14: Making bread rise
column15: Killing bacteria that cause infections
column16: Helping plants photosynthesize in dim light
column17: Killing viruses like the flu and the common cold
column28: Penicillin is an antibiotic that kills bacteria. Antibiotics do not work on viruses like the flu, which is the common mistake.
column29: Anti- means against. Antibiotics fight one kind of microbe.

column9: Which kingdom feature does a fungus share with a plant?
column14: It reproduces with seeds.
column15: It makes food by photosynthesis.
column16: Its cells have cell walls.
column17: Its cell walls are made of cellulose.
column28: Both fungi and plants have cell walls, but fungal walls are chitin while plant walls are cellulose. Thinking they share cellulose is the common mistake.
column29: Three choices are only true for plants.

column9: Which statement best explains why fungi are important in nature?
column14: They break down dead material so its nutrients can be reused.
column15: They are the main food source for most of the animals in a forest.
column16: They hold soil in place with their roots.
column17: They make most of the oxygen in the air.
column28: As decomposers, fungi return nutrients from dead things to the soil. Plants and algae make oxygen, not fungi, which is the common mistake.
column29: Think about what fungi do to dead leaves and logs.

column9: Which group of foods depends on a fungus to be made?
column14: Apples and carrots
column15: Yeast bread and blue cheese
column16: Rice and beans
column17: Milk and eggs
column28: Yeast makes bread rise, and a mold gives blue cheese its veins and flavor. The other choices are plant or animal foods made without fungi.
column29: Which foods use yeast or mold?

column9: A student says, "Mushrooms are plants because they grow in soil and don't move." Which evidence best shows the student is wrong?
column14: Mushrooms come in many colors, including white, brown, red and yellow.
column15: Mushrooms grow quickly after rain, faster than most plants can grow.
column16: Mushrooms have no chlorophyll, and their cell walls are chitin.
column17: Mushrooms can be eaten by people.
column28: Lacking chlorophyll and having chitin walls are real differences from plants. Growing after rain, color and being edible are true of plenty of plants too, so they are irrelevant evidence.
column29: Pick the evidence that a plant could never show.

column9: A baker mixes yeast, warm water and sugar in a cup. Ten minutes later the cup is foamy. What is causing the foam?
column14: The yeast spores are bursting open.
column15: The sugar is melting in the warm water.
column16: The yeast is breaking down the sugar and giving off carbon dioxide gas.
column17: The yeast is using the sugar and light to make oxygen by photosynthesis.
column28: Yeast ferments sugar and releases carbon dioxide bubbles. Yeast is a fungus with no chlorophyll, so it cannot make oxygen by photosynthesis; that is the common mistake.
column29: Yeast is alive and eating. What gas do living things give off when they break down sugar?

column9: Put the steps of how a fungus feeds in order, from first to last.
column14: Hyphae release digestive enzymes onto the food
column15: The enzymes break the food into small molecules outside the fungus
column16: The hyphae absorb the small nutrient molecules
column17: Hyphae grow into the food source
column28: The hyphae reach the food, release enzymes, the food is digested outside the fungus, then the nutrients are absorbed. Putting absorbing before digesting is the common slip.
column29: The fungus has to be touching the food before anything else can happen.

column9: Put the steps of bread mold growing on a slice of bread in order.
column14: Black spore cases form on upright threads
column15: A spore lands on a moist slice of bread
column16: Threads branch through the bread into a fuzzy mat
column17: A tiny thread grows out of the spore
column18: The cases burst and release new spores
column28: A spore lands, sprouts a first thread, the threads spread into a mycelium, spore cases form and then release new spores. Putting the spore cases before the threads spread is the common slip.
column29: The cycle starts and ends with spores.

column9: Two slices of the same bread are sealed in bags. Slice A is kept in a warm, dark cupboard and Slice B in the refrigerator. After a week, Slice A is covered in mold and Slice B has only a little. What is the best conclusion?
column14: Mold needs light to grow.
column15: Cold temperatures slow the growth of mold.
column16: The refrigerator killed every spore on Slice B.
column17: Mold only grows on certain brands of bread.
column28: The only difference was temperature, and the cold slice grew much less mold, so cold slows mold. Slice B still grew a little, so saying every spore was killed goes too far.
column29: What was different between the two slices?

column9: Under a microscope, an unknown organism has cells with nuclei and cell walls but no chloroplasts. It grows as branching threads through a dead leaf. It is most likely a –
column14: plant
column15: animal
column16: fungus
column17: bacterium
column28: Nuclei, cell walls, no chloroplasts and branching threads through dead material all point to a fungus. Cell walls make some students pick plant, but a plant would have chloroplasts.
column29: Which kingdom has walls but no chloroplasts and grows as threads?

column9: Which statement correctly compares a plant seed with a fungal spore?
column14: Fungi make seeds, and only plants make spores.
column15: A seed holds a tiny plant and stored food; a spore is usually one microscopic cell.
column16: Both contain a tiny plant inside, but a spore's plant has no stored food.
column17: Spores are larger than most seeds, because each one holds more stored food to grow on.
column28: A seed is a many-celled package with an embryo and food, while a fungal spore is usually just one tiny cell. Thinking spores are just small seeds is the common mistake.
column29: Which one can you see without a microscope?

column9: Foresters notice that pine seedlings grow better in soil taken from an old pine forest that is full of fungi. What is the best explanation?
column14: The fungi photosynthesize near the surface and give the seedlings extra food and water.
column15: The fungi trap and eat the insects that would otherwise chew on the young roots.
column16: Fungi on the roots help seedlings take in water and minerals, and get sugar in return.
column17: The fungi turn into new roots for the seedlings.
column28: These root partners are mycorrhizae: the fungus's hyphae act like extra root surface, and the plant pays with sugar. Fungi cannot photosynthesize, which rules out the extra-food choice.
column29: What can a plant give a fungus, and what can thin threads in soil give back?

column9: Shelf fungi on a dead oak and a puffball in a field belong to the same group of fungi. Which group?
column14: Club fungi
column15: Common molds
column16: Sac fungi
column17: Imperfect fungi
column28: Mushrooms, shelf fungi and puffballs are club fungi (Basidiomycota); they make spores on club-shaped cells. Sac fungi make spores in sacs, which is the common mix-up.
column29: This is the same group as the button mushroom.

column9: Baker's yeast and the morels that hunters find in Wisconsin woods each spring are in the same group. Which group?
column14: Common molds
column15: Club fungi
column16: Imperfect fungi
column17: Sac fungi
column28: Yeast and morels are sac fungi (Ascomycota), which make spores inside tiny sacs. Morels look like mushrooms, so picking club fungi is the common mistake.
column29: The group is named for where the spores are made.

column9: A fungus has only ever been seen reproducing asexually. Which group is it placed in?
column14: Sac fungi
column15: Club fungi
column16: Imperfect fungi
column17: Common molds
column28: Imperfect fungi are the ones known to reproduce only asexually. Molds, sac fungi and club fungi can reproduce both sexually and asexually.
column29: Which group is "missing" a way to reproduce?

column9: Which group of fungi causes most fungal diseases in humans, such as athlete's foot and ringworm?
column14: Sac fungi
column15: Imperfect fungi
column16: Common molds
column17: Club fungi
column28: In our notes, the imperfect fungi cause many human diseases like athlete's foot and ringworm. Club fungi are mostly mushrooms and shelf fungi, which is the common mix-up.
column29: It is the same group that includes Penicillium.

column9: Match each group of fungi to an example.
column14: Common molds :: Black bread mold
column15: Sac fungi :: Truffles
column16: Club fungi :: Button mushrooms
column17: Imperfect fungi :: Penicillium
column28: Bread mold is a common mold, truffles are sac fungi, button mushrooms are club fungi and Penicillium is an imperfect fungus. Mixing up sac and club fungi is the most common mistake.
column29: Start with the mushroom and the bread mold, then place the other two.

column9: Why do fungi make millions of spores at a time?
column14: Spores are needed to photosynthesize.
column15: Every spore must join with thousands of other spores before it can start to grow.
column16: Each spore turns into a seed, and seeds are fragile.
column17: Most spores land where there isn't enough food or moisture, so few survive.
column28: Spores spread randomly, and most land in bad places, so making huge numbers makes it likely a few succeed. Thinking spores are seeds is the common mistake.
column29: Think about where a spore might land after the wind blows it away.

column9: Many fungi grow very close to the ground, where a thin layer of still air sits. How do they get their spores past this still air?
column14: They grow seeds with wings.
column15: They only release spores at night, when the still air layer is gone.
column16: Some shoot their spores out; others use animals, water or wind.
column17: They wait for the ground to freeze.
column28: Fungi either shoot their spores past the still layer or rely on animals, water or wind. Fungi never make seeds, which rules out winged seeds.
column29: The spores need a push or a ride.

column9: A store manager throws out a whole loaf of bread when only one slice shows mold. Why is that a reasonable choice?
column14: Hyphae and spores may have spread into other slices out of sight.
column15: Mold only grows on the surface of one slice, so the store wasted a good loaf.
column16: The visible fuzz is the whole fungus, so the other slices in the bag are fine.
column17: Mold makes bread rise again in the bag.
column28: The fuzz you see is only part of the fungus; hyphae grow into the food and spores spread to nearby slices. Thinking the visible fuzz is the whole fungus is the common mistake.
column29: Where do hyphae grow?

column9: In a class lab, 24 slices of bread were left in warm, moist bags. After 5 days, 18 slices had visible mold. What percent of the slices grew mold?
column28: 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75, which is 75%. A common mistake is dividing 24 by 18 (about 133%), which can't be right because a percent of the slices can't be more than 100.
column29: Divide the number that grew mold by the total number of slices, then multiply by 100.

column9: Match each fungus to how it affects people or nature.
column14: Penicillium :: Source of a medicine that kills bacteria
column15: Oak wilt fungus :: A disease that kills oak trees
column16: Truffle :: A costly food that grows underground near tree roots
column17: Puffball :: Releases a smoky cloud of spores when pressed
column28: Penicillium gives us penicillin, oak wilt fungus kills oaks, truffles are prized food and puffballs release clouds of spores. Mixing up the helpful and harmful fungi is the common mistake.
column29: Two of these help people, one harms trees, and one is about reproduction.

column9: Which statement correctly compares hyphae and a mycelium?
column14: Hyphae grow above ground, and the mycelium is the mushroom cap.
column15: A mycelium is a mass made of many hyphae.
column16: Hyphae and mycelium are the fungus's roots and stem.
column17: A hypha is a mass made of many mycelia.
column28: Each thread is a hypha, and many tangled hyphae make a mycelium. Flipping the two is the most common mistake.
column29: Which is the single thread and which is the tangle?

column9: Which pair shows one way fungi help people and one way they harm people?
column14: Making bread rise; making penicillin
column15: Making penicillin; causing athlete's foot
column16: Making seeds; spreading pollen
column17: Causing ringworm; causing oak wilt
column28: Penicillin helps people, and athlete's foot harms them. Bread rising with penicillin are both helpful, ringworm with oak wilt are both harmful, and fungi make neither seeds nor pollen.
column29: Check each choice for one good thing and one bad thing.

column9: A bread mold's black spore cases burst, and a few days later mold appears on a bowl of fruit nearby. What most likely happened?
column14: The mold's roots grew across the counter to the fruit.
column15: Spores floated through the air and landed on the fruit.
column16: Seeds from the mold fell into the fruit bowl.
column17: The fruit made mold by itself as it ripened.
column28: Spores are tiny and light, so air carries them to new food. Fungi have no roots or seeds, and mold never appears without a spore or a piece of hypha to start it.
column29: What did the bursting cases release?

column9: Select every place where you would likely find fungi decomposing something. Select all that apply.
column14: An old orange at the back of the fridge
column15: A clean, dry glass window
column16: A pile of wet, fallen leaves
column17: A rotting stump in the woods
column19: A sealed, sterile can of soup
column28: Fungi decompose dead material that is moist, like stumps, wet leaves and old fruit. A sterile can, clean glass and new plastic give a fungus no food or moisture.
column29: Fungi need food and moisture. Which places have both?

column9: Which statement about how fungi get around is correct?
column14: Most fungi stay in one place and spread by growing hyphae and scattering spores.
column15: Fungi swim using hair-like cilia.
column16: Fungi pull themselves along with their roots, a few centimeters each day, like a slow vine.
column17: Fungi crawl using false feet.
column28: Fungi stay put and spread by growing and by releasing spores. False feet and cilia belong to protists, which is the common mix-up from the last target.
column29: Think of how mold reaches a new slice of bread.

column9: Which description best fits the cells that make up a mushroom?
column14: Many eukaryotic cells with chitin walls, packed together as hyphae
column15: One giant cell with no nucleus
column16: Many cells with chloroplasts and cellulose walls, packed together as tissue
column17: Prokaryotic cells stacked in layers
column28: A mushroom is tightly packed hyphae made of eukaryotic cells with chitin walls. Picking chloroplasts and cellulose describes a plant, which is the common mistake.
column29: Mushrooms are fungi. What do all fungal cells have?

column9: A student places a mushroom cap gills-down on white paper overnight. In the morning, there is a pattern of brown dust on the paper. What is the dust?
column14: Pieces of chitin falling off
column15: Spores released from the gills
column16: Pollen made by the cap
column17: Dried-up digestive enzymes
column28: This is a spore print: the gills drop millions of spores. Calling it pollen is the common mistake; fungi make spores, not pollen.
column29: What does the fruiting body make?

column9: Pigs and dogs are trained to find truffles underground by smell, and wild animals dig them up and eat them. How does this help the truffle fungus?
column14: The animals spread the truffle's spores in their droppings.
column15: It doesn't help; it only harms the fungus.
column16: The animals plant truffle seeds as they dig.
column17: The animals give the truffle sunlight when they dig it up.
column28: Truffles grow underground, so wind can't carry their spores. Animals eat them and spread the spores in their droppings. Fungi don't make seeds, which rules out planting seeds.
column29: Wind can't reach underground. What else can carry spores?

column9: Bacteria and fungi can both cause infections and both decompose dead things. Which feature puts fungi in a different kingdom from bacteria?
column14: Fungi can make their own food from sunlight, and bacteria cannot make any food.
column15: Fungi are always larger than any bacterium.
column16: Fungal cells have a nucleus (eukaryotic), and bacterial cells do not.
column17: Fungi have no cell walls, and bacteria do.
column28: Fungi are eukaryotes and bacteria are prokaryotes. Yeast cells are tiny, so size doesn't decide it, and fungi cannot make their own food, which rules out the food-making choice.
column29: Think about what is inside the cell.

column9: One fungus grows on a living maple tree and slowly kills it. A different fungus grows on a dead stump. Which labels are correct?
column14: Both are parasites
column15: Both are producers
column16: Living maple: parasite; dead stump: saprophyte
column17: Living maple: saprophyte; dead stump: parasite
column28: A parasite feeds on a living host and harms it; a saprophyte feeds on dead material. Swapping the two terms is the common mistake. Fungi are never producers.
column29: Which host is alive?

column9: In a class lab, mold grew fastest on homemade bread with no preservatives and slowest on store bread with preservatives. Which explanation makes the most sense?
column14: Homemade bread has more sunlight inside.
column15: Preservatives slow the growth of fungi on food.
column16: Store bread is made of plants, and homemade bread is not.
column17: Preservatives give mold extra food.
column28: Preservatives are added to food to slow the growth of molds and other microbes. Thinking homemade bread is somehow different in kind is the common mistake; both are made from flour.
column29: Why do companies add preservatives to bread?

column9: A swimmer keeps getting athlete's foot after wearing damp socks all day. Which advice best uses what you know about fungi?
column14: Dry the feet well and wear dry socks, because fungi need moisture.
column15: Plant the socks in soil to remove the fungus.
column16: Put the feet in sunlight so the fungus can't photosynthesize.
column17: Wear the same socks longer so the fungus gets used to them and stops growing.
column28: Fungi thrive in warm, moist places, so drying the skin takes away what they need. Fungi don't photosynthesize anyway, so blocking photosynthesis would not matter.
column29: What condition does the fungus need that you can take away?

column9: A new organism is many-celled and eukaryotic, absorbs nutrients from rotting wood, has chitin cell walls and reproduces with spores. A student argues it is a plant because ferns and mosses also make spores. Which is the strongest reply?
column14: Spores alone don't decide it; chitin walls and absorbing food show it is a fungus.
column15: The student is right, because anything that makes spores and grows on wood is a plant.
column16: It must be a protist, because it is eukaryotic.
column17: It must be an animal, because insects also use chitin.
column28: Some plants make spores too, so spores are not proof. Chitin walls and absorbing food are fungus traits. Being eukaryotic fits four kingdoms, and chitin alone doesn't make it an animal; animals have no cell walls.
column29: Which traits does this organism have that no plant has?

column9: A student wants to test whether moisture affects how fast bread mold grows. Which setup is a fair test?
column14: One slice of white bread misted in the fridge, and one slice of wheat bread kept dry on a warm counter.
column15: One slice misted with water, with nothing to compare it to.
column16: Two slices of the same bread at the same temperature in the dark; one misted and one kept dry.
column17: Two slices misted with water, one in the fridge and one on a warm counter.
column28: A fair test changes only moisture and keeps the bread, temperature and light the same. The white-versus-wheat setup changes three things at once, a single misted slice has no comparison, and the fridge-versus-counter setup tests temperature, not moisture.
column29: Only one thing should be different between the two slices.

column9: A single yeast cell is placed in warm sugar water. Every 90 minutes, each yeast cell buds and makes one new cell. If no cells die, how many yeast cells will there be after 6 hours?
column28: 6 hours is 360 minutes, which is 4 rounds of 90 minutes. The number doubles each round: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16. A common mistake is adding one cell each round or forgetting to convert hours to minutes.
column29: First find how many 90-minute rounds fit in 6 hours. Each round, every cell makes one more.

column9: A student measures the width of a mold colony on a small agar dish each day: Day 1: 4 mm, Day 2: 9 mm, Day 3: 15 mm, Day 4: 15 mm. What is the best explanation for Day 4?
column14: The hyphae shrank back into the original spore.
column15: The mold turned into a plant on Day 4.
column16: The mold ran out of food, space or moisture, so the colony stopped spreading.
column17: The mold switched to photosynthesis on Day 4, so it no longer needed to spread for food.
column28: Growth stops when hyphae run out of food, space or water. Fungi can't photosynthesize and don't turn into plants, so those choices misunderstand what fungi are.
column29: The dish is small. What would a growing fungus eventually run out of?

column9: Fungi are sometimes called "nature's recyclers." Which chain of events best explains the nickname?
column14: Fungi make spores → spores become soil → plants grow in the spores.
column15: Fungi photosynthesize → they make oxygen → animals breathe it.
column16: Hyphae release enzymes into dead matter → it breaks into small molecules → nutrients return to the soil.
column17: Fungi eat living plants → the plants die and rot away → new plants grow from the fungal seeds left behind.
column28: Fungi digest dead material outside their bodies, and the released nutrients become available to plants again. The other chains describe photosynthesis or seeds, neither of which fungi do.
column29: Recycling means taking something used up and making it usable again.

column9: Why does a fungus grow as long, thin, branching hyphae instead of as one solid lump?
column14: Thin threads spread out to catch as much sunlight as possible for photosynthesis, like leaves.
column15: Thin threads work like tails that let the fungus swim through water and wet soil.
column16: Thin, branching threads give a huge surface for releasing enzymes and absorbing food.
column17: Thin threads are used to hold seeds.
column28: A fungus feeds by absorbing through its surface, so spreading out as thin threads puts much more surface in contact with food. Thinking it is for catching light is the common mistake.
column29: A fungus feeds through the outside of its body. How would you get the most outside?

column9: A gardener sprays a chemical that kills every fungus in her garden soil. Which problem is she MOST likely to see over the next year?
column14: Her garden fills with more mushrooms than before, since the chemical feeds the spores.
column15: Her plants stop needing water.
column16: Her plants grow worse without their root-partner fungi, and dead leaves rot slowly.
column17: Her plants grow faster, because the fungi were stealing their sunlight and water.
column28: Fungi help roots take in water and minerals, and they decompose dead material. Removing them hurts plants and slows recycling. Fungi don't use sunlight, so they weren't stealing any.
column29: Think of two helpful jobs fungi do in soil.

column9: Penicillium makes penicillin, which kills bacteria. In nature, how might making penicillin help the mold itself?
column14: It kills nearby bacteria that compete with the mold for the same food.
column15: It helps the mold do photosynthesis.
column16: It attracts nearby bacteria so the mold can trap and eat them.
column17: It makes the mold's spores heavy so they land close by and grow near the parent.
column28: Bacteria and molds often feed on the same dead material, so killing bacteria leaves more food for the mold. It can't help photosynthesis because fungi don't photosynthesize.
column29: Bacteria and molds are both decomposers. What happens when two decomposers want the same food?

column9: A student lists reasons that fungi are NOT plants. Select every reason that is correct. Select all that apply.
column14: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin.
column15: Fungi digest food outside their bodies and absorb it.
column16: Fungi often grow in damp, shady places.
column17: Fungi are eukaryotic.
column28: Chitin walls, no chlorophyll and digesting food outside the body then absorbing it all separate fungi from plants. Plants are also eukaryotic and have cell walls, and mosses and ferns grow in damp shade too, so those traits don't tell them apart; choosing them is the common mistake.
column29: A good reason must be true of fungi and NOT true of plants.

column9: Select every statement that is true of BOTH fungi and animals. Select all that apply.
column14: Both have eukaryotic cells.
column15: Both are heterotrophs that get food from other organisms.
column16: Both reproduce mainly with spores.
column17: Chitin is found in fungi and in some animals, such as insects.
column18: Both digest food inside a stomach.
column19: Both have cell walls around their cells.
column28: Fungi and animals are both eukaryotic heterotrophs, and both groups use chitin (fungal walls, insect shells). Animal cells have no cell walls, fungi have no stomach, and animals don't reproduce with spores.
column29: Check each statement against a mushroom AND a beetle.

column9: Which comparison of a mushroom and a maple tree is correct?
column14: Both have cellulose cell walls, but only the maple has nuclei in its cells.
column15: Both make seeds, but only the mushroom absorbs its food.
column16: Both make their own food from sunlight, but only the mushroom has chitin walls.
column17: Both are made of many eukaryotic cells, but only the maple makes its own food.
column28: Both are multicellular eukaryotes, but only the maple photosynthesizes. Each wrong choice puts a plant-only trait (making food, cellulose, seeds) on the mushroom too.
column29: Check both halves of each choice. One wrong half makes the whole choice wrong.

column9: Put the events in the discovery of penicillin in order.
column14: Scientists purified the bacteria-killing substance into the medicine penicillin
column15: Fleming saw a clear zone with no bacteria around the mold
column16: A Penicillium mold spore landed on one of the dishes
column17: Fleming grew Staphylococcus bacteria on lab dishes
column28: The bacteria were growing first, a mold spore contaminated a dish, Fleming noticed the clear zone, and later scientists turned the substance into medicine. Putting the medicine before the clear zone is the common slip.
column29: Fleming had to notice something before anyone could make a medicine from it.

column9: Put the steps of a mushroom-forming fungus's life in order, starting with the release of spores.
column14: Threads grow from the spore and spread into an underground mass
column15: A spore lands on moist soil full of dead leaves
column16: After a rainy spell, a new mushroom pushes up out of the soil
column17: Spores drop from the gills of a mushroom cap
column28: Spores drop, land somewhere moist, grow into a mycelium, and the mycelium sends up a new fruiting body. Thinking the mushroom comes straight from the spore, before the underground mass, is the common mistake.
column29: The mushroom is the last thing to appear, not the first.

column9: Two forests each have a fallen tree of the same size. Forest A has warm, moist soil full of fungi. Forest B is cold and dry with few fungi. Where will the fallen tree likely break down faster, and why?
column14: Forest B, because cold kills the fungi that protect the wood.
column15: Forest B, because cold, dry air cracks and breaks wood down faster than fungi do.
column16: Forest A, because fungi decompose wood faster where it is warm and moist.
column17: They will break down at the same rate, because fungi don't affect wood.
column28: Fungi are major decomposers of wood and grow best when it is warm and moist. Thinking fungi protect wood, or have no effect, misses their role as decomposers.
column29: Where would fungi be most active?

column9: A honey fungus in an Oregon forest covers more than 2,000 acres, yet above ground you only see scattered clumps of mushrooms in the fall. What explains this?
column14: The fungus is mostly made of spores floating above the forest.
column15: The mushrooms are hundreds of separate fungi that just happen to grow close together in one forest.
column16: Most of it is a mycelium hidden in the soil and roots; the mushrooms are its fruiting bodies.
column17: The fungus covers 2,000 acres only when its mushrooms are up.
column28: One mycelium can spread underground over huge areas, and the mushrooms are just its reproductive parts. Thinking each mushroom is a separate organism is the common mistake.
column29: Where is most of a fungus's body?

column9: A student says, "Yeast can't be a fungus, because fungi are made of hyphae and yeast is only one cell." Which is the best response?
column14: The student is right; yeast is a bacterium, because it is only one cell and has no hyphae.
column15: The student is right; yeast is a protist, because protists are one-celled eukaryotes with no hyphae.
column16: Yeast is a one-celled fungus; like all fungi, it is a eukaryotic heterotroph with chitin walls.
column17: Yeast does have hyphae, so it is many-celled like other fungi.
column28: Being one cell doesn't rule out Kingdom Fungi; yeast shares the key fungal traits. Calling it a bacterium ignores its nucleus, and yeast does not normally grow as a mycelium of hyphae.
column29: Which traits do all fungi share, even yeast?

column9: An organism is eukaryotic and absorbs its food from dead material, but its cell walls are made of cellulose and it has cells that swim with flagella. A biologist says it is NOT a true fungus. Which evidence best supports her?
column14: Only plants can absorb food from dead material, so it must be a plant.
column15: True fungi always make their own food with chlorophyll, like plants.
column16: True fungi are always prokaryotic.
column17: True fungi have cell walls made of chitin, not cellulose.
column28: Cellulose walls are the giveaway; organisms like this are fungus-like protists (water molds). The other choices are false: fungi don't make their own food, aren't prokaryotic, and absorbing food is exactly what fungi do.
column29: Which fungal trait does this organism break?

column9: Scientists find a new fungus. Which question would help them most in deciding which of the four groups it belongs to?
column14: How, and in what kind of structure, does it make its spores?
column15: How big does it grow, and how fast does it spread?
column16: What color is its cap?
column17: Does it grow on dead wood, on soil, or on another living thing?
column28: Fungi are classified by the way they reproduce: how they form spores and the shape of the structure that makes them. Color, size and where it grows vary within each group.
column29: Fungi are sorted into groups by how they reproduce.

column9: A baker's bread dough didn't rise at all. Which reason is most likely, based on yeast being a living fungus?
column14: The yeast made too much oxygen.
column15: There was too much chitin in the flour.
column16: The dough was kept in the dark, so the yeast couldn't photosynthesize.
column17: The water used was so hot that it killed the yeast cells.
column28: Yeast is alive, and very hot water kills it, so no carbon dioxide is made and the dough stays flat. Yeast doesn't photosynthesize, so darkness isn't the problem.
column29: What can kill a living thing in the kitchen?

column9: A ring of mushrooms (a "fairy ring") appears in a lawn, and each year the ring gets a little wider. What best explains this?
column14: One mycelium grows outward underground, and mushrooms pop up along its growing edge.
column15: The grass in the center makes new mushrooms each year and pushes the old ones outward.
column16: Each mushroom drops seeds that land just outside the ring and sprout the next year.
column17: Mushrooms walk outward a little each year.
column28: The mycelium spreads outward through the soil like a ripple, and fruiting bodies appear at the active edge. Fungi don't make seeds, and mushrooms can't move.
column29: Picture the hidden body of the fungus spreading out in all directions.

column9: Match each observation to what it shows about fungi.
column14: Mold grows on bread in a dark cupboard :: Fungi do not need light to get food
column15: A lab test finds chitin in a mushroom's cell walls :: Fungal walls are different from plant walls
column16: Mushrooms pop up in a lawn a day after heavy rain :: Fruiting bodies form when there is enough moisture
column17: White threads grow deep inside a moldy peach :: Hyphae grow into the food source
column28: Each observation is evidence for one trait: growing in the dark shows fungi aren't photosynthetic, chitin separates them from plants, rain triggers fruiting bodies and threads inside food show hyphae feeding. Matching the dark cupboard to moisture is the common slip.
column29: Ask what each observation proves, not just what it describes.

column9: A student puts a few drops of enzymes taken from a fungus on a cube of cooked egg white. Overnight, the cube shrinks and the liquid around it gets cloudy. What does this best model?
column14: Fungi make food by photosynthesis.
column15: Fungi turn egg into spores.
column16: Fungi swallow their food whole and then digest it inside.
column17: Fungi digest food outside their bodies with enzymes.
column28: The enzymes broke down the egg outside any organism, just as a fungus digests its food outside its body before absorbing it. Nothing was swallowed or made by photosynthesis.
column29: The enzymes worked without the fungus even being there.

column9: A town wants its yard-waste compost pile to break down faster. Which change would most help the fungi in the pile?
column14: Cover it tightly with plastic so no air gets in, and let it dry out.
column15: Spread it thin in full sun until it is bone dry, so it breaks into small pieces.
column16: Keep the pile damp and turn it often so the fungi have moisture and air.
column17: Spray it with a chemical that kills fungi.
column28: Decomposing fungi need moisture and oxygen to grow. Drying the pile or killing the fungi slows decomposition, which is the opposite of the goal.
column29: What conditions help fungi grow?

column9: Some soil fungi trap tiny worms in loops of hyphae and then digest and absorb them. How does this fit the description of fungi?
column14: It still fits: the fungus digests the worm outside its body and absorbs it.
column15: It makes the fungus a plant, because a Venus flytrap also traps and digests animals.
column16: It shows that some fungi have mouths.
column17: It makes the fungus an animal, because it catches and kills moving prey.
column28: Catching prey doesn't change how the fungus eats: it still releases enzymes and absorbs the nutrients. Deciding the fungus is an animal because it catches food is the common mistake.
column29: How does the fungus actually take in the worm after trapping it?

column9: Two dishes of the same bacteria each get a different mold in the center. After 3 days, Dish 1 (Penicillium) has a clear zone with no bacteria around the mold, and Dish 2 (bread mold) does not. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: The clear zone was caused by bright light shining on Dish 1 but not on Dish 2.
column15: Penicillium makes something that stops these bacteria; this bread mold does not.
column16: All molds kill bacteria.
column17: Bread mold kills more bacteria than Penicillium, which is why Dish 2 has no clear zone.
column28: Only the Penicillium dish had a clear zone, so only that mold stopped the bacteria. Saying all molds kill bacteria goes beyond the evidence, since Dish 2 shows one mold that didn't.
column29: Compare the two dishes. What was different, and what happened?
